title: One Sound, More Than One Spelling: a_e and ay
overview:
New spellings: a_e, ay.
No new sound today. Two new ways to write one you know.
Two letters. One sound.
Do not sound them out one by one.
functions: Say the sound for each new spelling
Read a word that has one in it
Write a word that has one in it
Know where in a word each one goes
Read the new words out loud
Choose between two spellings of one sound
learningPath: Words: the new spellings and the new words.
Write the words from their sounds.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
lectureScript:
This is Unit 15. Book B starts here.
Book B has no new sounds at all.
Not one. You have them all.
What it has is new ways to WRITE them.
You know the long a. You met it as ai.
Rain. Wait. That is the sound.
Today you meet two more spellings.
The same sound. Written a different way.
The first is ay. Day. Pay. Away.
It comes at the end of a word.
Ai never comes at the end. Ay does.
That is the whole rule for that one.
The second one is stranger. Listen.
The word man. m. a. n. Short a.
Now I add an e at the end.
M. A. N. E. Mane.
The e is not said. It says nothing.
But it reaches back over the n.
And it makes the a say its name.
Man becomes mane. Tap becomes tape.
Cap becomes cape. Hat becomes hate.
We write this a_e. A, gap, e.
The gap is where one letter goes.
Name. n. a_e. m. Three sounds.
Not four. The e is silent.
Late. l. a_e. t. Three sounds.
So now you have three ways to write long a.
Ai in rain. Ay in day. A_e in name.
Which one does a word use?
You cannot hear it. You have to have seen it.
That is not a fault in you. It is English.
Read a lot and you will know.
That is Unit 15.

grammar.title: The new spellings: a_e, ay
grammar.explanation:
There is no new sound in this unit.
Long a is the sound. You already have it.
These are two more ways to write it.
grammar.rule:
a_e   as in name    n - a_e - m
ay    as in day     d - ay

Both say long a. So does ai, from Unit 13.
grammar.workedExample:
You see a_e in a word.
1. Do not read two letters.
2. Read one sound.
3. Say that sound out loud.
4. Now find it in name.
5. Say the sound again there.
grammar.mistake:
Sounding out both letters gives no word at all.
name is not n - a - m - e.
It is n - a_e - m.
grammar.tip: Two letters. Look once. Say once.
grammar.practice:
Say the sound for each one.
1. a_e
2. ay
grammar.answers:
Check yourself out loud.
Did you say ONE sound each time?
Two sounds means you read the letters, not the spelling.

grammar.title: Reading a word that has a_e, ay in it
grammar.explanation:
Find the two letters first.
Read them as one sound.
Then read the rest of the word.
grammar.rule:
name     n - a_e - m
late     l - a_e - t
day      d - ay
pay      p - ay
make     m - a_e - k
take     t - a_e - k
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word late.
1. Look for the two letters.
2. Cover them with your finger.
3. Read what is left.
4. Now put the one sound back in.
5. Join it all. late.
grammar.mistake:
Reading left to right, letter by letter, breaks here.
Look for the pair BEFORE you start.
grammar.practice:
Join the sounds and write the word.
1. n - a_e - m
2. l - a_e - t
3. d - ay
4. p - ay
5. m - a_e - k
6. t - a_e - k
grammar.answers:
1. name
2. late
3. day
4. pay
5. make
6. take
Five or six right? You can read these.

grammar.title: Writing a word that has a_e, ay in it
grammar.explanation:
Say the word. Break it into sounds.
One of those sounds needs TWO letters.
Count sounds, then write.
grammar.rule:
name     n - a_e - m        3 sounds, 4 letters
late     l - a_e - t        3 sounds, 4 letters
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write day.
1. Say it out loud.
2. Break it: d - ay.
3. Which sound needs two letters?
4. Write that pair together.
5. Read it back to check.
grammar.mistake:
One letter for each sound is wrong now.
The new sound takes two letters.
grammar.tip: Count sounds. Some need two letters.
grammar.practice:
Write the word you hear.
1. day
2. pay
3. make
4. take
5. away
6. game
grammar.answers:
1. day
2. pay
3. make
4. take
5. away
6. game
Five or six right? Good.

grammar.title: The e at the end reaches back
grammar.explanation:
A silent e at the end is not idle.
It reaches back over one letter.
It makes the vowel say its own name.
grammar.rule:
man   ->  mane
tap   ->  tape
cap   ->  cape
hat   ->  hate
not   ->  note
pin   ->  pine

The e is never said.
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word tape.
1. Look at the end. There is an e.
2. Count back one letter. That is the p.
3. The vowel before it is the a.
4. So the a says its name. Long a.
5. t - a_e - p. Tape.
grammar.mistake:
Saying the e is the mistake.
Tape is not tay-pee. The e does a job and stays quiet.
grammar.tip: A silent e makes the vowel long.
grammar.practice:
Add an e. What is the new word?
1. man
2. tap
3. cap
4. hat
5. not
6. pin
grammar.answers:
1. mane
2. tape
3. cape
4. hate
5. note
6. pine
Say each pair out loud. Short, then long.

grammar.title: Which spelling? ai, ay or a_e
grammar.explanation:
Three spellings. One sound.
The sound cannot tell you which.
But the POSITION can, a little.
grammar.rule:
ay    at the end        day, pay, away
ai    in the middle     rain, wait
a_e   middle, with e    name, late

No English word ends in ai.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write the word play.
1. Where is the long a sound?
2. It is at the end of the word.
3. So it is not ai. Never ai at the end.
4. Try ay. P - l - ay.
5. Play. That looks right.
grammar.mistake:
Waiting to hear which spelling it is.
You cannot. Use the position, then read to check.
grammar.tip: At the end, it is ay.
grammar.practice:
Which spelling? Write ai, ay or a_e.
1. r__n
2. d__
3. n_m_
4. w__t
5. p__
6. l_t_
grammar.answers:
1. rain (ai)
2. day (ay)
3. name (a_e)
4. wait (ai)
5. pay (ay)
6. late (a_e)
The two at the end are both ay. That is the one real rule.

readings.title: The New Job
readings.genre: A short text using known spellings
readings.setting: A first week at a new job
readings.passage:
I got a job today.
The man said his name.
I must not be late.
So I take the bus at six.
They pay me at the end of the week.
It is not a lot of pay.
But it is a job. I can make it.

readings.title: Three Ways, One Sound
readings.setting: The wall card, fourteenth one along
readings.passage:
Long a has three spellings.

ai    rain, wait     middle
ay    day, pay       end
a_e   name, late     middle, silent e

You cannot hear which. You learn it by reading.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The new sounds
speaking.instructions:
Listen and repeat each sound.
a_e
ay
ONE sound each. Not two.
Now say each one three times.
Tap the mic. Say them all.
Check: one sound, or did two slip out?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say one of the new sounds. Say it back.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Read the words
speaking.instructions:
Say each word two ways. Slow, then fast.
1. n - a_e - m ... name
2. l - a_e - t ... late
3. d - ay ... day
4. p - ay ... pay
5. m - a_e - k ... make
6. t - a_e - k ... take
Tap the mic. Say all six both ways.
Check: was the new spelling one sound?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say three sounds. Join them and say the word.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Say it, then write it
speaking.instructions:
For each word: say it, break it, write it.
1. day
2. pay
3. make
4. take
5. away
6. game
Tap the mic. Say each word and its sounds.
Check: did you say the sounds before you wrote?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word with the new spelling. Break it out loud.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Read the list
speaking.instructions:
Read these out loud, straight down the list.
name
late
day
pay
make
take
away
game
Do it twice. The second time, try not to stop.
Tap the mic. Read the list twice.
Check: was the second time easier?
speaking.tutor: Read the list to the tutor. Ask which words were not clear.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Short, then long
speaking.instructions:
Say each pair out loud, one after the other.
man, mane
tap, tape
cap, cape
hat, hate
The e is never said.
Tap the mic. Say all four pairs.
Check: did the second one have a long vowel?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say cap and cape. Say which has the e.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Say it, then spell it
speaking.instructions:
Say each word. Then say its long a spelling.
rain. day. name. wait. pay. late.
Say the word, then say ai, ay or a_e.
Tap the mic. Do all six.
Check: were the two ending words both ay?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word ending in ay.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Words with the new spelling
writing.prompt:
Say each word. Break it into sounds.
Write two letters for the new sound.
writing.criteria:
Six words.
The new spelling written as a pair.
You read each one back after writing it.
writing.extension: Now write one more word with the same spelling.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Sounds and letters
writing.prompt:
Write each word. Then write two numbers.
How many sounds. How many letters.
writing.criteria:
Six words.
Two numbers beside each one.
The numbers are not the same. That is the point.
writing.extension: Find a word where they ARE the same.

quizzes.why: Read the pair as one, not as two letters.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: n - a_e - m. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: The sounds in order make the word.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: l - a_e - t. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: Find the pair first, then read the rest.

quizzes.q: To write a word with the new spelling you ___.
options: write two letters for that sound
write one letter for each sound
quizzes.a: write two letters for that sound
quizzes.why: The new sound is one sound and two letters.

quizzes.q: How many sounds are in name?
quizzes.why: Count what you HEAR. There are more letters than sounds.

options: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.a: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.why: Letter by letter is the slow way here.

quizzes.q: You cannot read a word. What do you do first?
quizzes.why: Find the pair, then read around it.

quizzes.q: Add an e to the word tap. It becomes ___.
quizzes.why: The e reaches back and makes the a long.

quizzes.q: In the word name, the e at the end is ___.
quizzes.why: It is never said. It changes the vowel instead.

quizzes.q: Which long a spelling goes at the END?
quizzes.why: No English word ends in ai.

quizzes.q: You cannot hear which spelling a word uses. So you ___.
options: read a lot and learn it
quizzes.a: read a lot and learn it
quizzes.why: The spelling is seen, not heard.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

This is the whole unit, and it goes against everything Units 2 to 7 taught. Expect a learner to read the letters separately for a while. Do not explain it again; point at the pair and say the one sound, and have them say it back. It is a habit, and habits are built by repetition, not by argument.

teacherNotes.type: Find the pair before reading, not during
teacherNotes.note: Left-to-right letter-by-letter reading breaks on these words, because the learner commits to the first letter's sound before they have seen the second. The move is to scan the word for the pair first. A finger under the pair is enough. It looks like a crutch and it is the skill.

From here to the end of the level there are always more letters than sounds. A learner who counts letters will write a spare letter into every word. Have them say the word and count on their fingers before they write.

teacherNotes.type: Say it before they notice it: there is no new sound here
teacherNotes.note: A learner who expects a new sound will listen for a difference between rain and name, hear none, and think their ears have failed. Open the unit by saying Book B adds no sounds at all. It turns the hardest thing about these five units into the easiest thing to understand.

teacherNotes.type: The silent e is an action, not a leftover
teacherNotes.note: Adults often learn it as a rule about what e does NOT do. Teach it as something it DOES: it reaches back one letter and makes the vowel say its name. Say the pairs — man mane, tap tape — and have the learner hear the change rather than recite the rule.

teacherNotes.type: The choosing question has no full answer, so do not pretend it does
teacherNotes.note: Position gives one real rule — ay at the end, never ai — and beyond that the spelling has to have been seen. Say so. A learner who is waiting for a rule stalls on every word; one who knows the truth just reads more.

assignment.title: Read and write the new words
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Record yourself. Say the sound for each new spelling.
Then read these words, slowly and then faster:
name, late, day, pay, make, take
2. Write six of the words from their sounds.
Beside each one, write how many sounds it has.
Listen back before you finish.
